ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short to medium turns, with a long, presentation-style monologue followed by brief questions and extended, exploratory answers. Early conversation is casual and loosely organized, with frequent greetings, small talk, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), occasional audio/logistics checks, and several false starts or self-corrections. Speakers use many hedges and thinking markers—“um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “you know,” “maybe,” “I guess”—especially when posing interpretations or unanswered questions. The overall register is collegial and semi-informal despite the technical setting: introductions are more formal, while discussion quickly becomes conversational and appreciative. Participants build on one another by referencing prior questions, affirming points before adding caveats, and framing challenges as curiosity rather than confrontation; disagreement is indirect and usually expressed as uncertainty or an alternative explanation. Questions tend to be prefaced with praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “just curious”), often arrive in multi-part, somewhat improvised form, and may include repetitions as the speaker formulates the thought.

Meeting style for this meeting (polite_friction): Courteous but with real tension. People disagree in an indirect way: with a question, a hedge, a long pause, or 'let's take that offline'. Some disagreements are dropped rather than resolved. Nobody raises their voice.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I mean, that could work. I'd just want to see it on our data first.
  - Sure. We can park that and come back to it.
  - Right. I'd still like to know how you'd handle the late ones, but okay.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Assessing whether forest carbon credits actually protect forest and who gets to decide how that is measured.

speakers.name: Dr. Marisol Vega
speakers.background: Forest landscape ecologist with 14 years of experience evaluating avoided-deforestation and restoration projects in tropical and subtropical forests. She combines repeated forest inventories, plot-based biomass measurements, satellite time series, and spatial analysis of forest-cover change. She has worked with project teams and public agencies to assess counterfactual baselines, displacement of clearing to nearby areas, and risks that credited carbon will be released through fire, logging, or later conversion.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Her opening question is: "Do credited projects reduce forest loss relative to a defensible baseline, once we account for leakage and permanence?" She treats a credit's ecological claim as testable against observed forest conditions and credible counterfactuals, while recognizing that baseline choices, monitoring boundaries, and what counts as forest can alter the answer. She wants forest inventory and remote-sensing evidence to remain central, but sees a need to understand why different institutions authorize different measurements and assumptions.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Kwame Mensah
speakers.background: Comparative political scientist with 16 years of experience researching land governance, decentralization, environmental regulation, and extractive and conservation projects in rural regions. His work uses comparative case analysis, policy and legal document analysis, elite and community interviews, and process tracing to examine how formal rules interact with customary authority and enforcement capacity. He has advised public agencies and civil-society organizations on tenure reforms and benefit-sharing arrangements.
speakers.distinct_perspective: His opening question is: "How do land tenure, authority, enforcement, and the distribution of decision-making power shape forest-carbon project outcomes?" He approaches carbon projects as governance arrangements rather than neutral interventions: rights to land and carbon, control over monitoring, bargaining power in contracts, and the ability to enforce restrictions determine whose forests are protected and who bears costs. He will press the group to treat ecological effectiveness as inseparable from the institutional arrangements that authorize projects and allocate power.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Rahman
speakers.background: STS scholar with 11 years of experience studying environmental accounting, audit systems, participatory mapping, and the circulation of expertise in climate governance. She conducts ethnographic observation, interviews with technicians and local residents, document tracing, and analysis of methodological standards to follow how measurements become authoritative facts. Her previous work examined how satellite classifications, field observations, community testimony, and audit reports are translated into tradable environmental claims.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Her opening question is: "How are ecological observations and local knowledge converted into quantified credits through methodologies, auditors, certifiers, and decisions about what counts as valid evidence?" She is interested in the practical chain through which a forest becomes a number: category definitions, data templates, verification visits, audit judgments, and the exclusion or reinterpretation of local accounts. She is skeptical of treating measurements as simply given, but can help bridge the team toward a shared question about how credit effectiveness is jointly defined, measured, and governed without displacing the ecological or political questions.

benchmark_task: Give a meeting with three disciplines, each opening with a different research question, that loosely converge on a shared question. The evaluated AI must capture the bridging question while preserving all three disciplinary sub-questions.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting with three disciplines, each opening with a different research question, that loosely converge on a shared question. The evaluated AI must capture the bridging question while preserving all three disciplinary sub-questions.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting with one ecologist, one political scientist, and one STS researcher. At the opening, each participant must state a distinct disciplinary research question. The ecologist's question must concern whether credited projects reduce forest loss relative to a defensible baseline, including leakage and permanence and evidence from forest inventory or remote sensing. The political scientist's question must concern how land tenure, authority, enforcement, and the distribution of decision-making power shape project outcomes. The STS researcher's question must concern how ecological observations and local knowledge are converted into quantified credits through methodologies, auditors, certifiers, and decisions about what counts as valid evidence. During discussion, participants should recognize that credit effectiveness cannot be assessed separately from the institutions and measurement practices that define and govern it. They should loosely converge on a shared bridging question, but retain the three original sub-questions as necessary components rather than collapsing them into one discipline's framing. They may identify a need to compare cases, but should not finalize sites, methods, hypotheses, or literature recommendations.

ground_truth.bridging_question: How do forest carbon credit projects' ecological claims of avoided forest loss become measured, verified, and governed, and how do those measurement and governance arrangements shape whether forests are protected and who has authority over that determination?

disciplinary_subquestions.ecology: Do credited forest carbon projects reduce forest loss relative to a defensible counterfactual baseline, after accounting for leakage and the permanence of claimed carbon benefits, as assessed through forest inventory and remote sensing?
disciplinary_subquestions.political_science: How do land tenure, the allocation of authority among states, local communities, and project actors, and the capacity to enforce rules shape forest carbon project outcomes and control over decisions?
disciplinary_subquestions.science_and_technology_studies: How are baseline estimates, forest observations, and local knowledge translated into carbon-credit numbers through methodologies, auditors, and certifiers, and whose evidence is treated as authoritative in that process?

ground_truth.required_connection: The formulation must make measurement and verification part of the causal and political problem, not treat ecological impact as an independent technical fact. It must preserve ecological additionality, governance and authority, and the construction and validation of credit numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. I hope we can leave today with a question that doesn't treat the carbon estimate as separate from the institutions producing it, who has authority over land, over the rules, and over what becomes credible evidence. We don't need to settle cases today, obviously, but I'd like to understand where each of you sees that connection most, um, sharply.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: What I most want is for us not to take the credit number as the starting fact. I keep coming back to the chain of small decisions, decisions about what counts as forest, which observations enter the baseline, and what an auditor accepts. And that can make a selectively logged area disappear from the account while residents are saying it is damaged. So authority over evidence seems inseparable from authority over land here.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I'd want us to hold onto the physical forest outcome alongside that chain. If a project reports avoided loss, we need to ask, avoided relative to what, and whether clearing has just moved beyond the mapped boundary or biomass has declined under a canopy that still gets counted as forest. Aisha, do the audit rules usually say much about what residents' observations can change in those classifications?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Mm, where does that enter?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: It enters unevenly, I think. Most schemes have a consultation or grievance channel, but that is not the same as treating a resident's account as evidence that can revise a canopy classification or a baseline. I'd want to trace the actual procedure and the auditor's discretion. Marisol, when your plots and the satellite layer disagree, what usually decides the final call?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: It depends on the protocol, but usually the remotely sensed layer is the first screen, and the plots are used to calibrate it or check it. If they conflict, though, it shouldn't just come down to picking the cleaner-looking dataset. We need to ask whether canopy cover is masking degradation, or whether the plots are too sparse. That's partly why I'd want the audit trail. Who was allowed to call that disagreement material?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: That phrase, “material,” is doing a lot of work. I’d want to know who gets to make that call, and whether a disagreement has to fit a prescribed data form before it can even get to the auditor. And Marisol, are there kinds of plot evidence that would actually force a reclassification under the usual protocols, or does the canopy threshold more or less hold?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Before we treat the reclassification threshold as the decisive hinge, I'd want to know who controlled ground access for those plots, and who could contest the resulting map. A technically valid protocol can still ratify a very particular distribution of authority if customary boundary claims or restrictions on residents' access never become, um, material evidence in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: And that could change the ecological inference, not just its legitimacy. If plot access follows only the project's recognized boundaries, we may miss places where clearing or degradation is being displaced. Kwame, with overlapping customary claims, have you seen that affect which areas monitors can actually enter?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Quite often. Recognized project boundaries can effectively become the boundaries of observation, even where seasonal use, lineage claims, or customary corridors cut across them. Monitors may be admitted through the office-holding chief, but not by households with a competing claim. I’d want us to distinguish denied access from forest that’s genuinely inaccessible, because those lead to very different inferences about displacement and about whose account of the boundary the project has already made authoritative.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: That distinction is really important. From the forest side, I'd need an access map almost as much as a forest-change map, showing where plots or field checks could happen, where they couldn't, and why. Otherwise, a quiet area outside the boundary may just be an unobserved area. And how do we tell whether a small clearing belt reflects displacement, versus people finally being visible to the monitoring system?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: I don't think we can infer that from the pattern alone. We would need the chronology, when the restriction, patrol, or benefit arrangement began, who used that belt beforehand, and whether people could plausibly shift there under their own tenure claims. Otherwise, um, "newly visible" may mean the project has changed whose land use is legible, and that's not a neutral baseline problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Hm, the chronology matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: And the chronology is also a chronology of the categories, not just land use. If a belt becomes visible only after a boundary, a patrol route, or a new baseline template, then the later map can make it look like a new ecological event. I wonder if we should follow those changes together, together with when the forest changed and when the project’s way of seeing it changed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: I'd add the chronology of who could make a category stick. A boundary or baseline template may change not just observation but bargaining power. Once a use is coded as encroachment, households may have very little room to contest it. So maybe the question is whether changes in forest condition, measurement practice, and local authority co-produce the credited outcome, instead of treating them as three parallel histories, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s the knot, isn’t it?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I’d want the question to still let us test the outcome, though, not just how it was produced. Maybe when a project credits avoided loss, how do changes in authority and measurement affect both the reported baseline and what actually happens to forest condition inside and around the boundary? Then we can see whether the three histories line up, or whether, say, the credit survives while biomass or clearing patterns tell a different story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: I think that is close, but I would resist putting authority just as something that affects the baseline. It also determines who can refuse restrictions, negotiate benefit-sharing, or make a grievance consequential, so it may shape the forest outcome directly. Could we say, how do evolving authority arrangements and measurement practices shape the reported and realized forest effects of credited avoided loss, within and beyond project boundaries?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Mm, yes—realized effects.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: That wording works, as long as “reported” lets us examine the machinery that makes a report credible, not just compare it with a separate realized outcome. We should ask whether the documents are actually available to trace that- whether we can get method revisions, verification reports, and responses to objections. Otherwise authority becomes something we infer after the fact.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Before we choose regions, I’d want to check whether those records exist in a form we can actually compare, especially baseline revisions, verification findings, and any mapped monitoring gaps. Otherwise we could make a very elaborate claim about how authority shaped the result and still not know whether the reported avoided loss holds up against the, um, forest evidence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: I’d put one more screen ahead of comparability. Whether the legal and contractual record lets us identify who held the carbon right, who authorized access, and what remedies existed when a boundary was disputed. Otherwise, a region can look wonderfully document-rich while the decisive allocation of authority sits in an unpublished agreement or, frankly, in customary practice that no verification file records.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: I'd be cautious about treating missing agreements or customary practice as just a documentation gap, though. It may be exactly how some decisions are kept off the auditable record. So maybe our initial case screen needs to ask both what we can obtain and what remains deliberately or routinely unrecorded, because otherwise the archive, the archive starts setting the limits of the authority story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: For the ecological side, an absence in the record has to be a finding we carry forward, not a blank we quietly smooth over. We can screen for whether the satellite record and any inventories let us independently see inside, outside, and across the access gaps. But if access or agreements are withheld, that limits what we can say about displacement rather than making it...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: And I’d want the screen to treat that limitation substantively, not just, um, can we get documents, but can we reconstruct the effective authority arrangement from contracts, administrative decisions, and competing local accounts. If a carbon right or enforcement mandate is opaque, that may make a case harder, but it’s also central to the question, so we shouldn’t select only the unusually legible projects.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Yes—opacity should be a comparison variable, not just a reason to exclude a case.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, I can live with that, as long as opacity doesn't mean we give up on checking the forest outcome. Maybe the case screen should deliberately include variation, one relatively transparent project and one where authority or records are harder to see, but only where the imagery and some independent ground evidence can still, um, show us what happened inside and around the boundary.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Kwame Mensah
transcript.text: Yes—variation, but we should not equate opacity with absence of governance.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're at time. This was really useful, so let's pick this up once we've had a chance to look at what records and forest data are realistically available. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Thanks, all. Bye.
